content: Early aggressive behavior in children is recognized as a significant risk factor for future violence and criminal activity. Despite over two decades of implementing violence prevention programs in schools, there remains uncertainty about the effectiveness of various interventions specifically targeting children who exhibit aggressive tendencies. The objective of this study was to evaluate the impact of school-based violence prevention programs on children identified as aggressive or at risk of becoming aggressive. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including CENTRAL, the Cochrane Injuries Group specialized register, MEDLINE, EMBASE, and other specialized sources. Additionally, reference lists of relevant articles were reviewed, and authors and organizations were contacted to identify any additional studies. The inclusion criteria for the trials were as follows: participants had to be randomly assigned to either intervention or control groups; outcome data needed to be collected concurrently; participants were required to be children in mandatory education who were identified as exhibiting or being at risk of aggressive behavior; interventions had to be designed to address aggression, violence, bullying, conflict, or anger; the interventions had to be school-based; and the outcomes measured included aggressive behavior, school or agency responses to aggression, or violent injuries. Data were systematically collected on study design, participant characteristics, intervention details, outcomes, and indicators of study quality. The results of interventions were compared to no intervention, both immediately after the intervention and at a 12-month follow-up, using meta-analysis when appropriate. Out of 56 trials identified, none provided data on violent injuries. However, aggressive behavior was significantly reduced in intervention groups compared to control groups immediately after the intervention. This finding was based on 34 trials with available data, yielding a standardized mean difference (SMD) of -0.41 (95% confidence interval [CI]: -0.56 to -0.26). This reduction in aggressive behavior was sustained at the 12-month follow-up, as reported in seven studies, with an SMD of -0.40 (95% CI: -0.73 to -0.06). School or agency disciplinary actions in response to aggressive behavior were also reduced in intervention groups, as evidenced by nine trials with available data (SMD = -0.48; 95% CI: -1.16 to 0.19). However, this difference may have been due to chance, and the reduction was not maintained in the longer term, as shown by two studies reporting follow-up data at two to four months (SMD = 0.03; 95% CI: -0.42 to 0.47). Subgroup analyses suggested that interventions focusing on improving relationship or social skills might be more effective than those teaching non-response strategies to provocative situations. Additionally, the benefits of these interventions were similar regardless of whether they were delivered to primary or secondary school children, or to mixed-sex groups versus boys-only groups. In conclusion, school-based secondary prevention programs aimed at reducing aggressive behavior appear to result in significant behavioral improvements beyond what would be expected by chance. These benefits are observed across different age groups and gender compositions. However, further research is necessary to determine whether these programs can reduce the incidence of violent injuries and whether the observed benefits can be sustained beyond 12 months.
